messages.subject: MAR and NMAR missing
parts:
Hi, Dr. Phil,


I have two different missing values patterns in my data (two different educational tests). The first one is NMAR (not missing-at-random), and the second one is MAR (missing-at-random), as can be seen in the pictures. My question is: can I set 'mirt' package to NMAR or MAR to estimate the items parameters? My data is dichotomous, N > 1,000.

I think that because time was very short to do all 110 items, NMAR can be observed.


Thanks a lot,

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: MAR and NMAR missing
parts:
On Thu, Dec 4, 2014 at 4:10 PM, Danilo Assis Pereira <dani...@gmail.com> wrote:

Hi, Dr. Phil,


I have two different missing values patterns in my data (two different educational tests). The first one is NMAR (not missing-at-random), and the second one is MAR (missing-at-random), as can be seen in the pictures. My question is: can I set 'mirt' package to NMAR or MAR to estimate the items parameters? My data is dichotomous, N > 1,000.

I think that because time was very short to do all 110 items, NMAR can be observed.

You're right there is definitely a time effect going on here, where after about the 60th item missingness seems to consistently increase. However, this in and of itself may not be an issue depending on the missingness mechanism, and MAR could very well be a reasonable assumption (which is mirt's default). Let me explain.

If the only reason individuals have difficulty answering those last items is because of individual differences in the time it takes to answer items, then MAR is a reasonable assumption and the estimation would simply take into account that there are less observations for those items, and in turn their parameter sampling variability will be much higher (i.e., have higher standard errors). However, if there is a reason other than time that is responsible for these missing data patterns, then MNAR is an issue. More specifically, for example: are the students with higher abilities more likely to answer those last few questions compared to the rest of the students? Lower ability students more likely? Is there any visual relationship between the score estimates and missing data pattern? Etc. The point is that time by itself really is not an issue in MAR here, it's whether some individuals are more likely to response based on their innate ability. And if there are observable biases based on the latent trait scores, then MAR is being violated and there's little you can do about it without making some rather dogmatic assumptions. If MAR is violated, you may have to count your losses and discard the last half of the test.

My suggestion would be to continue to look into the problem using regression-based methods. Perhaps using the first 60 items only, compute latent trait estimates for individuals and try and discern whether there is a relationship to the probability of attempting the items in the last half of the test. If the relationships end up being small or insignificant, then MNAR may not be an issue and the MAR assumption is still fairly reasonable. 

Note that for policy reasons, you probably should also look at other demographic variables as well to see if they predict the missingness (i.e., were males more likely to answer more questions than females, primary speaking language more likely to answer more, etc). Though these really don't effect the parameter estimation, directly in order to justify keeping them for the future you would want those to be non-significant as well (otherwise you'd bias the number of items administered for one sub-population over another...which is difficult to justify). Good luck.

Phil
Thanks a lot,
